faqs.answer: The corners. A circle inside a square leaves four curved gaps empty, and those gaps are about 27 percent of the square. The square pan fills them in, so it holds about 27 percent more batter at the same depth.
faqs.question: Why does the square hold so much more?

faqs.answer: They brown faster than the middle, because heat reaches them from two sides. They will not burn at the recipe time, but check the cake 5 minutes early the first time, and tent the pan with foil if the corners darken before the center sets.
faqs.question: Will the corners burn?

faqs.answer: Yes. A 9-inch square recipe baked in a 9-inch round scales by 0.79, since 63.6 divided by 81 is 0.79. The round pan holds about a fifth less, so scale down or bake the extra batter separately.
faqs.question: Can I go the other way, square to round?

faqs.answer: Not at the same depth. The crumb bakes the same. The corners are firmer and chewier than the middle, which is why brownie lovers fight over them, but the cake itself is unchanged.
faqs.question: Does the shape change the texture?

faqs.answer: Yes, it is the classic brownie pan. Brownies are cut into squares, and a square pan wastes no edges. The same 1.27 factor applies to a round brownie recipe moving into the square.
faqs.question: Is a 9-inch square the right pan for brownies?

felicityNote: The square pan is the brownie pan for a reason. Those corners are the best part, and the maths is the price of them.

formula.text: New batter = recipe batter x 1.27. Factor = new area divided by old area = 81 divided by 63.6 = 1.27.

howToSteps.name: Work out the factor
howToSteps.text: A 9-inch square covers 81 square inches and a 9-inch round covers 63.6. Divide 81 by 63.6 and the factor is 1.27.

howToSteps.name: Scale every ingredient
howToSteps.text: Multiply each ingredient by 1.27, including the leavening. A recipe with 5 cups of batter becomes 6.4 cups.

howToSteps.name: Check the fill
howToSteps.text: Pour the scaled batter into a greased 9-inch square pan. It should sit between half and two-thirds full, no higher than about 6.7 cups.

howToSteps.name: Bake as the recipe says
howToSteps.text: Same oven temperature, same bake time. Test the center with a toothpick, and check 5 minutes early the first time because the corners set fast.

title: 9-Inch Round to 9-Inch Square Pan
tutorial: The difference between a round pan and a square pan of the same size is the corners. A 9-inch round covers 63.6 square inches. A 9-inch square covers 81, because the corners fill in the four gaps the circle leaves empty. Those corners add about 27 percent more floor, and the batter has to grow by the same amount to keep its depth.

A 9-inch round recipe makes about 5 cups of batter for one layer, and scaled by 1.27 that becomes 6.4 cups in the square pan. A 9-inch square holds 10 cups to the rim, so 6.4 cups sits comfortably under the two-thirds fill line, which is about 6.7 cups. A recipe that makes 6 cups becomes 7.6, which is over two-thirds, so check the fill before the pan goes in the oven.

Pour the round recipe into the square pan without scaling and two things happen: the cake bakes thinner, and the corners set first. Corners get heat from two sides at once, so they brown faster than the middle. On a thin, unscaled cake the corners can go from golden to dry while the center is still setting. Scaling fixes the depth, and the corners still brown first, so check the cake 5 minutes early the first time.

The square pan earns its keep for bars and brownies, where straight sides and neat corners are the point. A round cake cut into squares wastes the curved edges. A square cake cut into squares wastes nothing. If the recipe is a brownie or a blondie, the square pan is the better pan anyway, and the 1.27 factor is the price of the corners.

Bake at the same temperature and the same time. Both pans are 2 inches deep and the scaled batter sits at the same depth, so the middle sets on the same schedule. Test the center with a toothpick, not a corner. The corners will always test done first, and trusting them means an underbaked middle.
